# Bush Expresses "Deep Concern" Over Quran Desecration in Call to Iraqi Prime Minister

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush conveyed his profound concern and expressed regret to Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki regarding the desecration of a Quran by an American soldier, the White House announced Tuesday.

According to al-Maliki's office, President Bush addressed the incident during a phone call with the Iraqi leader. National Security Council spokesman Gordon Johndroe confirmed that Bush spoke with al-Maliki on Monday during one of their regularly scheduled secure video teleconferences.

"President Bush expressed his deep concern over the incident and told Prime Minister Maliki that the soldier has been reprimanded by his commanders and removed from Iraq," Johndroe stated.

Al-Maliki's office reported Tuesday that Bush had formally apologized on behalf of the United States and "promised to present the soldier to the courts." The apology, according to the office, was delivered during a Tuesday morning phone call between the two leaders.

## Background on the Incident

The controversy stems from an American staff sergeant—serving as a sniper section leader—who used a Quran for target practice in Iraq earlier this month. The U.S. commander in Baghdad issued a formal apology on Saturday, during which he read aloud a letter of contrition from the soldier responsible.

Military officials confirmed that the sergeant has been relieved of his duties as section leader "with prejudice," officially reprimanded by his commanding general, dismissed from his regiment, and reassigned back to the United States.

News of the desecration has sparked outrage among Muslims both within Iraq and across the globe. According to villagers, the soldier fired at the Quran on May 9, though the bullet-riddled text was not discovered until two days later, the military reported.

A local tribal leader described the incident as "the criminal act by U.S. forces," noting it occurred at a shooting range near the Radhwaniya police station on Baghdad's western outskirts. After the soldiers departed, an Iraqi policeman discovered a target marked at the center of the bullet-ridden Quran. Photographs of the damaged text reveal numerous bullet holes alongside an expletive scrawled across one of its pages.

While officials noted that the soldier claimed ignorance of the book's identity, U.S. officials dismissed this explanation as implausible.

## Formal Apology Delivered

On Saturday, Maj. Gen. Jeffery Hammond, commander of U.S. forces in Baghdad, appeared alongside tribal leaders from Radhwaniya to deliver a personal apology.

"I come before you here seeking your forgiveness," Hammond told the assembled tribal leaders and community members. "In the most humble manner I look in your eyes today and I say please forgive me and my soldiers."

Hammond also read aloud a letter from the soldier responsible, who characterized his actions as "shortsighted, very reckless and irresponsible," while maintaining that malicious intent was never present. "I sincerely hope that my actions have not diminished the partnership that our two nations have developed together," the letter read.

The general characterized the soldier's conduct as tantamount to "criminal behavior," stating: "I've come to this land to protect you, to support you—not to harm you—and the behavior of this soldier was nothing short of wrong and unacceptable."

During the ceremony, another military official presented tribal leaders with a Quran as "a humble gift," kissing the sacred text beforehand as a gesture of respect.

## Iraqi Leaders Demand Stronger Action

Despite these gestures, many Iraqi leaders have made clear that an apology alone will not suffice.

On Monday, the Iraqi Islamic Party—the political movement led by Vice President Tariq al-Hashimi—condemned the incident as a "blatant assault on the sanctities of Muslims all over the world." The party stated it had reacted to the news "with deep resentment and indignation" and called for the "severest of punishments" to be imposed.

"What truly concerns us is the repetition of these crimes that have happened in the past when mosques were destroyed and pages of the holy Quran were torn and used for disgraceful acts by U.S. soldiers," al-Hashimi said. He further emphasized: "I have asked that first this apology be officially documented; second a guarantee from the U.S. military to inflict the maximum possible punishment on this soldier so it would be a deterrent for the rest of the soldiers in the future."

*CNN's Ed Henry and Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed to this report.*
